title: How to Talk so Teachers will Listen
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: Starting from a real Facebook post in which a teacher asks whether to follow UFLI or her school's phonological awareness PD, the author argues that being right about the research is not enough to change a teacher's practice. She dissects three actual replies: one that shares a similar story and gently introduces the evidence, one that scolds the teacher to just trust the program, and one that summarizes a specific paper and points to pages. The first and third are held up as models, the second as counterproductive. She then distills do and don't rules: use personal experience, be specific and conversational, ask questions, dignify careful questions with careful answers, and avoid condescension, us-versus-them framing and unexplained recommendations. The practical point is that persuading colleagues is a relational craft, and social media is where much of that professional conversation now happens.
points: Telling teachers the correct answer is not the same as changing their practice, because they are people with beliefs and feelings rather than algorithms.
The best replies build trust first by sharing a similar experience and only then introduce the research without being pushy.
Responses that cast colleagues as bad guys for not trusting evidence are likely to backfire even when they reach the right conclusion.
If you share research, summarize it and point to the relevant pages instead of just dropping a link.
The dos and don'ts (be specific, assume good faith, do not condescend) are a usable standard for professional conversations about practice.
quotes: We do want to encourage this teacher to proceed with UFLI and stop doing phonological awareness work in small groups. But we need to say more than that. We need to remember that the teacher asking these questions is an actual human being with beliefs and feelings, not a robot who will incorporate your instructions into their teaching algorithm.

I love this response. It reassures the teacher that she is not alone. This is a common misconception. In fact, there’s another teacher out there who had the same experience as she did! This connection immediately builds trust and creates a permission structure and model for the teacher to adjust her instruction. In addition, this response gently introduces the research underlying the recommendation, without being pushy and pedantic.

On the other hand, I hate this response. It judges the teacher and her colleagues and casts them as the bad guys for “trying to reinvent the wheel” and avoiding an evidence-based approach. Ironically, I’m sure the first and second posters would agree on the desired outcome: keep UFLI; ditch phonological awareness instruction. But this response is likely counterproductive.

Generally, I’m skeptical that sharing research articles is going to change teachers’ minds about instructional practices. But if you’re going to share research articles, use response three as a model: summarize the research and direct the teacher to the relevant pages.

I begin by remembering that the poster is open to learning and growth. Otherwise, she wouldn’t have asked the question this way. We should honor her intelligence and curiosity by talking to her like we would talk to a colleague, not by attacking her as though she were the enemy.
Social media is where these questions are being asked and answered all the time. We need to meet teachers where they are–on social media.
